On September 19, 2025, they forced their way into the family’s home in Grant, a small city outside Minneapolis, kidnapped the father and his family, and demanded access to his cryptocurrency accounts. # Crypto kidnappers who stole $8M from Minnesota family plead guilty

Crypto kidnappers who stole over $8 million from a Minnesota family after a violent home invasion have pleaded guilty, marking one of the largest U.S. cases of its kind. The brothers, Isiah and Raymond Garcia, held the family at gunpoint for more than eight hours, forcing them to surrender their cryptocurrency in a brutal "wrench attack."

Isiah Angelo Garcia, 25, and Raymond Christian Garcia, 24, both of Waller, Texas, pleaded guilty Thursday to interference with commerce by robbery. The plea was entered before U.S. District Judge Ann Montgomery in Minneapolis, [according to a Justice Department statement](https://cointelegraph.com/news/crypto-kidnappers-who-robbed-a-minnesota-family-of-8m-plead-guilty).

The brothers traveled from Texas to Minnesota with the sole purpose of robbing the family, prosecutors said. On September 19, 2025, they forced their way into the family’s home in Grant, a small city outside Minneapolis, kidnapped the father and his family, and demanded access to his cryptocurrency accounts. The victims were zip-tied and held at gunpoint for more than eight hours while the brothers forced the father to transfer funds. At one point, Isiah Garcia escorted the man to a family cabin in northern Minnesota to retrieve additional crypto storage devices, ultimately stealing over $8 million.

The family’s son managed to call 911, prompting the brothers to flee. Investigators later tracked them to the Houston area using evidence left at the scene, including surveillance footage and firearms. Both brothers admitted to using guns to threaten the family during the ordeal.

The Garcia brothers’ case is the latest in a disturbing rise of "wrench attacks," where criminals use violence or threats to force crypto holders to surrender their digital assets. Wrench attacks have become increasingly common in the U.S. and Europe. Wrench attacks often begin with meticulous planning. Criminals identify targets through social media, crypto forums, or even leaked transaction data. They then use deception—such as posing as delivery drivers or service technicians—to gain access to victims' homes. Once inside, they employ physical force, threats, or torture to extract private keys and wallet information.

### Why Crypto Holders Are Prime Targets

Cryptocurrency’s pseudonymous nature and irreversible transactions make it an attractive target for criminals. Unlike traditional bank transfers, crypto transactions cannot be reversed, leaving victims with little recourse once funds are stolen. This has emboldened criminals to use extreme measures, including kidnapping and torture, to extract private keys and wallet information.
